post.title: Fractal Lab
post.hook: A git log becomes a tree: every commit hash decides how one branch grows.
post.summary: A Next.js canvas playground for fractals (Mandelbrot, Julia, Burning Ship, Sierpinski, fern, tree) plus a Commit Journey page that grows a fractal tree from a repo's real git history.
post.writeup:
## What it is
Fractal Lab is a Next.js 16 and React 19 app with two pages. The home page is an interactive canvas playground with six fractal modes: mandelbrot, julia, burningShip, sierpinski, fern and tree. It has four palettes (Aurora, Ember, Prism, Noir), iteration and node budget controls, mirror symmetry and quadrant visibility toggles.

The second page, `/journey`, is a Commit Journey: it grows a fractal tree from a repository's real commit history.

## Why
The playground is a place to explore fractal math. The journey page turns project history into a visual artifact, so a repo's growth can be seen rather than read.

## How it works
A route handler at `/api/commits` runs `git log --no-merges --reverse --shortstat` on a requested repo path and parses author, date, subject, additions, deletions and files per commit. The limit defaults to 200 and is clamped to 1000.

Each commit hash is mapped to growth traits by a pure function: branch angle, left and right length ratios, lean, twist and a base hue. The same commit always grows the same way. Branch angle spans 14 to 48 degrees. The journey can be colored by journey, author or palette, and it plays back as an animation with sample data as a fallback.

Shared primitives (palettes, clamp, seeded hash-noise, an HSL to RGB conversion for fast canvas writes, escape-time coloring) were extracted into `lib/engine.ts` so both pages render with the same core.

## Findings
The deterministic hash-to-trait design works well: no stored state is needed, and identical history yields an identical tree. The folder is not a git repo, so there is no development timeline to report.

## Open questions
Large histories are capped by a segment budget of 60000, so very long repos will need sampling. Author-based coloring could also be extended to file-level signals.
